raw_case_text:
A 5 year and 4 month old boy was referred to us for polydipsia and polyuria. His blood glucose was 29.5 mmol/L, hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) was 8.9%, and fasting C-peptide was 0.07 ng/ml. Serum anti-glutamate decarboxylase antibody and anti-islet cell antibody were both positive. He was diagnosed with T1DM at the onset. He had a history of recurrent oral mucocutaneous Candida fungi and respiratory infections after birth. At the age of 1 year, he suffered from herpetic pharyngitis with alanine transferase (ALT) 1,000-2,000 U/L, which was relieved by anti-infective and liver-protecting treatment. Increased ALT levels occurred several times after infection. A left under axillary abscess incision and drainage was performed when he was 3 years and 8 months old. He was the first child of non-consanguineous parents without any family history of hereditary diseases.
Physical examination showed the weight was 18 kg (25th percentile), and the height was 110 cm (25th percentile). The blood pressure was normal. He was conscious, his thyroid and cardiopulmonary systems were normal, and there was no evidence of an enlarged lymph node. The liver is 4 cm under the right rib, and the spleen is 5 cm below the left rib, with blunt edges, and there is no swelling in the lower limbs.
Laboratory investigation revealed normal blood routine analysis, thyroid function, immunoglobulin A (IgA), immunoglobulin M, immunoglobulin G, ammonia, lactic acid, blood amino acids, acylcarnitine, and urine organic acid analysis. The level of aspartate aminotransferase was 100 U/L, ALT was 16.2 U/L. Hepatophilic virus antibodies [anti-cytomegalovirus-immunoglobulin M (CMV-IgM), anti-Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-IgM, hepatitis A/B/C/E virus antibodies] and autoimmune liver disease antibodies were negative. The thyroglobulin antibody, thyroid peroxidase antibody, and thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibody were negative. The percentage of CD4 lymphocytes was 21%, CD8 lymphocytes was 45%, and CD4/CD8 was 0.46, which indicated immunodeficiency, the detailed laboratory information was shown in Table 1.
WES identified a heterozygous de novo STAT1 mutation in the child, c.866A > G, p.Y289C, which was further confirmed by Sanger sequencing (Figure 1). It was previously shown to be a GOF mutation and was defined as pathogenic according to criteria published by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). The child was corrected diagnosed with monogenic autoimmune diabetes.
Based on the presence of CMC, immunodeficiency, autoimmune diabetes, and autoimmune hepatitis, as well as genetic results, the boy was diagnosed with syndromic CMC that was caused by a heterozygous GOF mutation of STAT1.
Upon admission, he was given rapid-acting insulin with meals and long-acting insulin at bedtime, with a total amount of 1.27 IU/kg/d, with blood glucose levels of 6-7 mmol/L before meals and 6-12 mmol/L after meals. During the follow-up, he was given oral antifungal therapy of fluconazole (75 mg/d) and intravenous injection of human immunoglobulin once a month for candidiasis and recurrent infections.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-4-month-old boy was referred for new-onset polydipsia and polyuria accompanied by severe hyperglycemia (29.5 mmol/L).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born to non-consanguineous parents, the child had a lifelong history since birth of recurrent oral mucocutaneous candidiasis (thrush), recurrent respiratory tract infections, recurrent episodes of post-infectious transaminitis (including ALT 1,000-2,000 U/L during herpetic pharyngitis at age 1 year), and a left axillary abscess requiring incision and drainage at age 3 years 8 months, before presenting at age 5 years 4 months with acute polydipsia, polyuria, severe hyperglycemia, and hepatosplenomegaly.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC) and recurrent respiratory tract infections since infancy, herpetic pharyngitis with severe acute hepatitis at age 1 year, and left axillary abscess incision and drainage at age 3 years 8 months; unremarkable family history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for polydipsia, polyuria, and recurrent oral thrush; negative for peripheral edema.

objective.physical_examination: Weight 18 kg (25th percentile), height 110 cm (25th percentile), normal blood pressure, alert sensorium, normal thyroid and cardiopulmonary examinations, no palpable lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly (liver palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and spleen palpable 5 cm below the left costal margin with blunt margins), and no lower-extremity edema.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood glucose 29.5 mmol/L, HbA1c 8.9%, fasting C-peptide 0.07 ng/mL, positive anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) and anti-islet cell autoantibodies, AST 100 U/L, and ALT 16.2 U/L. Complete blood count, thyroid function tests, serum IgA/IgM/IgG levels, plasma ammonia, lactate, tandem mass spectrometry blood amino acids and acylcarnitines, and urine gas chromatography-mass spectrometry organic acids were all normal. Serologies for anti-cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM, anti-EBV IgM, hepatitis A/B/C/E viruses, autoimmune hepatitis autoantibodies, and thyroid autoantibodies (anti-TG, anti-TPO, TRAb) were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral blood lymphocyte subset analysis demonstrated T-cell dysregulation with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.46 (CD4+ T cells 21%, CD8+ T cells 45%). Trio whole-exome sequencing (WES) with Sanger sequencing confirmation identified a pathogenic de novo heterozygous gain-of-function missense mutation in STAT1: c.866A>G (p.Y289C; both parents were wild-type).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Syndromic chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC), cellular T-cell immunodeficiency, autoimmune-like hepatosplenomegaly/hepatitis, and monogenic autoimmune type 1 diabetes mellitus caused by a de novo heterozygous STAT1 gain-of-function mutation (c.866A>G, p.Y289C; active cytomegalovirus [CMV], EBV, and viral hepatitis A/B/C/E excluded). Managed with subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin therapy (1.27 IU/kg/day achieving pre-prandial blood glucose levels of 6-7 mmol/L), daily oral fluconazole (75 mg/day), and monthly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) replacement.
